title: All My Sons
wpTitle: Reviews of All My Sons in the West End starring Bryan Cranston, Marianne Jean-Baptiste & Paapa Essiedu

ratings.excerpt: The stars of a dream cast align for Arthur Miller’s towering tragedy … Bryan Cranston, Marianne Jean-Baptiste, Paapa Essiedu and Hayley Squires achieve theatrical alchemy in Ivo van Hove’s superb production … Lightning has struck twice with this magnificent, shuddering production of Miller’s 1946 play … Ingenious tweaks render it a radically different experience. Miller’s three acts come with an interval but this runs straight through at a pace that is reminiscent of ancient Greek theatre in its fateful tragedy. … Van Hove, known for giving the classics his own stamp, steps back here, it seems, letting the cast (and what a cast this is) not just inhabit their parts but somehow become them as if by magic. … ... it is a rare thing to see a group of actors quite this brilliant gel so complete

A decade after his landmark ‘A View from the Bridge’, director Ivo van Hove strikes gold with another Arthur Miller play … To some extent the secret of his triumph here is ‘cast really really good actors’, foremost Bryan Cranston and Paapa Essiudu, who offer two of the best stage performances of 2025. But what van Hove has done is discretely uncouple Miller’s play from the naturalism that often stifles it. … Van Hove stages All My Sons like a series of playlets that flow into each other, the central drama slowly building to a climax but with each component given its due. It’s bound together by an extraordinary creative team … But it’s the actors that ultimately make it. An astonishing, deeply moving piece of theatre … Bryan Cranston, Marianne Jean-Baptiste and Paapa Essiedu are pitch perfect in this Arthur Miller revival … Bryan Cranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste deliver near pitch perfect performances as Joe and Kate Keller, a husband and wife shutting out unbearable wartime truths, in Ivo van Hove’s searing, morally forceful revival of Arthur Miller’s 1946 play. … Jean-Baptiste is magnificent as Kate, consumed by grief and conflicting emotion. Cranston is also superb as a superficially affable man lying to himself. … Essiedu is riveting to watch as Chris moves from pent-up apprehension to bafflement and then rage. Bryan Cranston is superb in a stupendously well-acted All My Sons … Ivo van Hove’s production of Arthur Miller’s play at Wyndham’s Theatre, London, lays bare the American dream … ... a stupendously well-acted production from Ivo van Hove, led by an outstanding Cranston with Paapa Essiedu (as his son, Chris) and Marianne Jean-Baptiste (as his wife, Kate) matching him step for step. … It was his stark 2014 staging of A View from the Bridge that put van Hove on the map in the UK, brilliantly paring away realism to reveal the bones of a Greek tragedy beneath. The director takes the same approach with All My Sons … Van Hove overdoes some elements: the atmospheric music sometimes feels unnecessary. But it’s the performances that strike home. Bryan Cranston is magnetic in this masterful staging of Arthur Miller’s tragedy … Ivo van Hove’s production follows a decade on from his other landmark Arthur Miller revival, 2015’s ‘A View from the Bridge … There’s an almost unbearable heaviness to Ivo van Hove’s powerful revival of All My Sons, staged with a crushing gravity underneath a giant glowing sun … Marianne Jean-Baptiste has profound depths as this mother who’s unable to face reality … Essiedu delivers a characteristically stellar performance as a younger brother who’s high on the drug of righteous optimism. … Van Hove manages something ingenious here, creating a version of suburban American that’s abstract and epic – while still humming with the sense of a local community

Bryan Cranston is magnificent in All My Sons … Cranston is a shoo-in for an Olivier for this immensely powerful production at Wyndham’s Theatre … ... Cranston offers a magnificent performance of craggy, rugged resilience tempered with affability in Arthur Miller’s 1947 classic. He’s matched for excellence by Marianne Jean-Baptiste, Paapa Essiedu and Hayley Squires, as this tremendous quartet unfolds a narrative of the almighty clashing of tides, with capitalism taking on ethics, fathers squaring up to sons and the past jostling for position with the future. … ... playing now at just over two hours without interval, All My Sons assumes the grim yet towering momentum, inexorability and universality of a Greek tragedy. … Designer Jan Versweyveld, Van Hove’s long-time partner in art and life,

Bryan Cranston breaks bad in Miller’s masterpiece … The American star is on strong form in Ivo Van Hove’s full-blooded version but it’s Paapa Essiedu who steals the show … Cranston gives a masterclass in fusing an easy exterior with a roiling interior … Good as everyone is here, it’s Paapa Essiedu... as Chris you walk out talking about. His ascent from affable shrugs to righteous rants is plausible, compelling, freshly minted. … ... this is a seriously good play, seriously well acted, seriously well staged.

Breaking Bad’s Bryan Cranston makes a magnificent West End debut … Cranston leads a superb cast in this powerful staging of Arthur Miller’s 1947 drama All My Sons … ... the virtue of this production is again its spare focus. … As Kate, Marianne Jean-Baptiste is transfixing, oddly tactile, palpably distracted: a mother who refuses to accept that her son has died, presiding over a family stuck in a limbo state of strained normality and withheld grief. … Paapa Essiedu confirms his star quality by bringing to Chris a combination of boyish charm, shrewd watchfulness and flaring passion. … With performances this strong, and a tragic climax so potent, the cinematic incidental music that plays beneath the dialogue feels like an unnecessary emotional nudge. Breaking Dad! Bryan Cranston put through the wringer in this tale of family despair … Not only does Miller supply heavyweight subject matter, his play is given a solemn, emotionally charged makeover by Belgian director Ivo van Hove … This, though, is a stark, ceremonial production. Cranston's casting as businessman Joe Keller is critical. … Jean-Baptiste is brilliant, too, as his conspiring wife who refuses to give up on the idea that her missing son might one day return. … The dirge-like atmosphere is sustained by plangent music and funereal laments by Johnny Cash and Leonard Cohen.  The result is a harrowing journey into guilt-racked despair. Like it or not, it's what keeps audiences and actors coming back to this play so often.

Brutal dismantling of the American dream … Bryan Cranston and Marianne Jean-Baptiste star in a shattering take on the Miller tragedy … His staging, lavishly cast and designed by his regular collaborator Jan Versweyveld, is shot through with a profound disgust for the jettisoning of morals and common humanity in the pursuit of the mighty dollar. As it builds towards a frenzy of anguish over more than two interval-free hours, you can’t help but sense a boiling anger at the current US administration. … Van Hove directs with his habitual expressionistic flourishes, some of which are a touch heavy-handed. … But the relationships between the characters are exquisitely drawn. In Cranston and Essiedu’s father-son connection, we see deep affection, but also frustration and a shadow of mistrust … In

Bryan Cranston in an explosive production … ...  it is what happens around Cranston’s crumbling paterfamilias Joe Keller that makes it so intense. … Other van Hove signatures are also on display, most notably the over-insistent music in Tom Gibbons’ sound design and snatches of songs between acts. But clear too is his remarkable ability to crank up tension, to pull the relationships in the Keller family to taut breaking point and to orchestrate the results. … Essiedu is simply superb, leaning into Colin’s essential goodness, his trust in a world that is about to be destroyed. … The sense of lives dashed is overwhelming. Van Hove risks a great melodramatic gesture at the close, but his production doesn’t need it. It has demanded that attention must be paid from the very start.
